item.title: Adaptive Collective Decision-Making in Signed Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.27147v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Collective decision-making often unfolds in networks where cooperation and antagonism coexist. Such signed interactions arise in social, biological, and robotic systems, and can lead to qualitatively different collective outcomes: consensus, polarization, or clustering. Existing signed network models typically explain these outcomes separately, leaving open how they can emerge within a single dynamical framework. Here, we introduce a generalized Laplacian flow for bi-partitioned signed networks, a class of networks that allows cooperative and antagonistic interactions both within and across two prescribed groups. The proposed model includes an adaptive social effort state, interpreted as a leaky memory of persistent signed network disagreement, which enables bounded and nontrivial steady-states beyond classical signed Laplacian flows. We derive conditions that determine whether the network reaches consensus, polarization, or clustering based on the spectral structure of the generalized Laplacian and effective resistance matrices. The framework applies beyond structurally balanced, weakly balanced, and quasi-structurally balanced networks, and reveals how changes in signed interaction strengths can shift a network between collective decision regimes. We validate the theory on stochastic block model networks, a judicial voting network, and a U.S. senate bill co-sponsorship network. Altogether, our results provide a structural and dynamical account of how mixed cooperative and antagonistic relationships shape emergent collective behaviors.
item.dc:creator: Vishnudatta Thota, Aditi Saxena, Twinkle Tripathy, Vaibhav Srivastava

item.title: How coalition size shapes bill cosponsorship in the U.S. Congress
item.description: arXiv:2611.27565v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Legislation is built by coalitions, yet studied through pairwise ties. Using five decades of U.S. House and Senate cosponsorship (1973-2025), we represent each bill as a group. Prior ties to current members predict who joins better than ties to the sponsor, and group history (earlier co-appearance with pairs of those members) produces a larger likelihood gain than sponsor ties alone. Coalition formation therefore retains a social memory of earlier groups: cooperation is organized around relational histories embedded in the coalition already assembled, which sponsor-cosponsor ties alone cannot recover. Completed coalitions also recur and share subgroups more often than degree- and size-preserving nulls predict. Party sorting peaks in coalitions of a few dozen members; as Congress polarized, small coalitions retained their cross-party share while mid-size coalitions became more partisan. Women are over-represented chiefly in coalitions led by Democratic women, although same-gender sponsor matching is close to zero after adjustment.
item.dc:creator: Bernardo Pereira, Giulia Preti, Andrea Santoro, Gianmarco De Francisci Morales, Giovanni Petri

item.title: Citizen-informed scenarios to shape energy demand reduction strategies
item.description: arXiv:2611.27834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Growing evidence has demonstrated the important role that energy demand reduction can play in achieving net zero. Despite this, the adoption of such measures in government strategies often remains limited, in part based on perceived public resistance to change. Using a novel combined deliberative-modelling approach, which fills a key gap in the literature, we find this is unfounded. Citizens both recognise the importance of and support demand-side interventions to achieve the UK's net-zero goals. This support, however, is conditional. If policy interventions can make demand-side choices practical and fair, we find citizens are prepared to reduce energy demand by at least 37% between 2025 and 2050, providing 20% of the abatement required to meet net-zero targets. Policymakers could thus unlock a wide range of demand reduction measures by acting on a more comprehensive understanding of public views and needs. Moreover, our approach offers a powerful framework, applicable in other contexts, to underpin policymaking with socially-informed quantitative modelling.
item.dc:creator: Andy Yuille, Oliver Broad, John Barrett, Christian Brand, Alice Garvey, Jonathan Norman, James Price, Steve Pye, Rebecca Willis

item.title: Network versus market information in coupled opinion-return dynamics
item.description: arXiv:2611.27874v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When making investment decisions, investors can use common signals from the market and local signals from their social networks. We develop an agent-based opinion-return model in which agents follow fixed trading strategies and respond to either local network information or a common market signal. In our model, trend followers and contrarians select either a local network signal or a common market signal and then update their buy, hold, or sell opinions by following or opposing the signal, respectively. The aggregate opinion imbalance determines the return, which sets the market signal. We find that three collective regimes emerge depending on how much network information is used and the fraction of contrarians in the population. Persistent directional states occur when trend followers dominate, market-wide reversals appear when a contrarian-rich population relies on the common market signal, and opposing opinions coexist with small aggregate returns when the same population relies on network signals. With a common market signal, the majority strategy has the higher payoff scores, whereas increasing reliance on network signals reduces this difference. When only network information is used, higher network clustering is associated with greater polarisation and smaller return magnitudes when trend followers dominate. Degree heterogeneity has little effect on aggregate measures but changes the payoff scores of high- and low-degree agents. In contrarian-rich populations, local information thus reduces aggregate return fluctuations even as opposing opinions persist.
item.dc:creator: Yue Yu, Luis Enrique Correa Rocha

item.title: Cup and cap synchronization: higher-order node dynamics from topology
item.description: arXiv:2611.16979v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Higher-order node-based synchronization provides distinct mechanisms for discontinuous synchronization transitions. However, a comprehensive theoretical framework capable of encompassing existing models and revealing the role of higher-order interactions beyond triangles is still missing. Here, combining algebraic topology and nonlinear dynamics, we introduce Cup and Cap Synchronization, a unifying theoretical framework for higher-order node-based dynamics that naturally incorporates the topological organization of the underlying higher-order network. We show that Cup and Cap Synchronization can display critical behavior belonging to the universality classes of two existing higher-order Kuramoto-like models, whose distinct critical behaviors were thought to originate from different mechanisms. Remarkably, we demonstrate that Cup and Cap Synchronization displays additional phenomenology not captured by the previously proposed models of higher-order node-based synchronization. Most relevantly, the inclusion of four-body interactions can fundamentally alter the critical properties of the synchronization transition, giving rise to collective phenomena that cannot be observed in models including only interactions mediated by edges and triangles. These findings reveal the importance of going beyond the commonly studied three-body terms and establish Cup and Cap Synchronization as a unifying theoretical framework for understanding collective dynamics in higher-order networks.
item.dc:creator: Runyue Wang, Yuanzhao Zhang, Ginestra Bianconi

item.title: The Fiscal and Economic Implications of Green Mandates: a Boltzmann Approach to Public Governance
item.description: arXiv:2611.27923v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Public authorities increasingly need to translate multifaceted policy objectives into concrete fiscal and investment choices while accounting for their socioeconomic consequences. A credible ex-ante impact assessment should report downstream implications attributable to the historical baseline and specified policy targets, without introducing discretionary assumptions about unknown administrative, socioeconomic or other physical processes. Bringing the large-scale perspective of statistical physics to public governance, we construct such an ex-ante impact assessment. Its scope encompasses policy objectives that condition a finite number of generalized moments of observables in the historical baseline, which comprises a sufficiently large collection of projects or public programmes. As a proof-of-principle application, we consider the green transition in the energy-generation sector using the historical baseline of many infrastructure projects from the World Bank. Our earlier results deriving closed-form expressions for coarse-grained combinatorial probabilities enable a tractable statistical and downstream assessment. We assess the statistical compatibility of the historical baseline with different levels of green-power surplus and demonstrate how the same statistical-physics construction can estimate any downstream metric expressible through arbitrary functions of generalized moments of the baseline observables. In the absence of more detailed knowledge about the processes forming the historical baseline, large-scale universality, whenever many unknown influences on collective phenomena become negligible, unambiguously offers a principled route to a self-contained ex-ante impact assessment.
item.dc:creator: Katerina Savvaidou, Georgia Foudoukidou-Louka, Ho-Ryun Chung, Orestis Loukas

item.title: Binary Decision Process in Pre-Evacuation Behavior
item.description: arXiv:2508.08284v5 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In crowd evacuation the time interval before decisive movement towards a safe place is defined as the pre-evacuation phase, and it has crucial impact on the total time required for safe egress. This process mainly refers to situation awareness and response to an external stressors, e.g., fire alarms. Due to the complexity of human cognitive process, simulation is used to study this important time interval. In this paper a binary decision process is formulated to simulate pre-evacuation time of many evacuees in a given social context. The model combines the classic opinion dynamics (the French-DeGroot model) with binary phase transition to describe how group pre-evacuation time emerges from individual interaction. The model parameters are quantitatively meaningful to human factors research within socio-psychological background, e.g., whether an individual is stubborn or open-minded, or what kind of the social topology exists among the individuals and how it matters in aggregating individuals into social groups. The modeling framework also describes collective motion of many evacuee agents in a planar space, and the resulting multi-agent system is partly similar to the Vicsek flocking model, and it is meaningful to explore complex social behavior during phase transition of a non-equilibrium process.
item.dc:creator: Peng N. Wang, Peter B. Luh, Peter Sincak, Laura Pitukova, Xuesong Lu, W. M. Wonham, Timo Korhonen

item.title: Trajectory-based cycle-level pedestrian crash prediction at intersections: A novel non-linear link function for block maxima led Bayesian GEV framework addressing heterogeneous traffic conditions
item.description: arXiv:2510.12963v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This study develops a cycle-level framework for estimating pedestrian crash risk at signalized intersections under heterogeneous, non-lane-based traffic. Existing approaches often assume linear relationships between covariates and parameters, oversimplifying the complex, non-monotonic interactions among motorized vehicles (MVs), non-motorized vehicles (NMVs), and pedestrians. To address this limitation, the framework introduces a non-linear link function within a Bayesian generalized extreme value (GEV) structure to capture how traffic effects vary. It applies extreme value theory through the block maxima approach using post-encroachment time as a surrogate safety measure, with each signal cycle serving as an analysis block. It also proposes a behaviour-normalized modified crash risk (MRC) metric to account for pedestrians' habitual risk-taking behaviour in Dhaka's mixed traffic. Seven hierarchical Bayesian models were estimated using Markov Chain Monte Carlo simulation and compared using the deviance information criterion. Models with a non-linear link function only in the GEV location parameter fit the data better than their linear counterparts. Results suggest pedestrian speed is negatively associated with crash risk, while flow and speed of MVs, pedestrian flow, and NMV conflicting speed show positive associations, though all remain uncertain. The selected model's MRC estimate was close to the observed crashes at a 93% confidence level tuned to this dataset. These results suggest that the non-linear structure adds flexibility for capturing the non-stationary and non-linear nature of traffic extremes. This framework is a step towards proactive identification of pedestrian crash risk and after wider validation, it could support adaptive signal control and safety interventions in mixed-traffic environments.
item.dc:creator: Parvez Anowar, Nazmul Haque, Md Asif Raihan, Md Hadiuzzaman
